title: Bones and joints: the hard frame inside you, and where it bends

summary.text: Press on your shin, then on your tummy. One feels hard and one feels soft. The hard part is bone. A grown-up has about 206 bones inside. A place where two bones meet is a joint, and that is where you bend. Your child shines a torch on the wall and moves one joint at a time, to find which joints can draw a circle and which can only draw a line.
summary.art: A girl of 7 in a dark room holding a torch with a straight arm, drawing a big circle of light on the wall, while a grown-up holds a second torch and watches.

intro.hook: Bend one finger slowly. How many places does it bend? Why does it not bend everywhere, like a piece of string?
intro.text: Hold out your hand and wiggle your fingers. Now press the back of one finger. It feels hard inside. That hard part is bone. Your finger can only bend in a few places. In this unit you find your bones by feeling them. You find your joints, where bones meet. Then you test which joints can move in a circle.
intro.art: A child's hand held up close, one finger bent, with three small dots of sketch pen on the three places where the finger bends.

outcomes: By the end I can say that I have bones inside me, and find some of them by pressing gently.
By the end I can say what a joint is, and show the joints in my finger, arm and leg.
By the end I can say that some joints, like my shoulder, move in a circle, and some, like my elbow, move only one way, like a door.
By the end I can say three jobs of bones: holding me up, keeping soft parts safe, and letting me move.
By the end I can say that muscles pull on bones to move them, and feel a muscle get hard when it works.
By the end I can say that bones are alive, and that a broken bone can mend.

terms.meaning: A bone is a hard, strong part inside your body. Bones are alive, and they grow as you grow.
terms.example: Press the front of your leg below the knee. The hard part you feel is your shin bone.
terms.art: A child pressing two fingers on the front of their lower leg, with a faint drawing of the shin bone under the skin.

terms.meaning: Your skeleton is all your bones together. It is the hard frame inside your body.
terms.example: A grown-up has about 206 bones in their skeleton. A crow, a cat and a fish have skeletons too.
terms.art: A friendly drawing of a whole human skeleton standing, with a small crow skeleton beside the feet.

terms.meaning: A joint is a place where two bones meet. Most joints let you bend or turn.
terms.example: Your elbow, knee, wrist and knuckles are joints.
terms.art: An arm bent at the elbow, with a circle drawn round the elbow joint.

terms.meaning: A hinge joint moves only one way and back, like a door on its hinges.
terms.example: Your elbow and knee are hinge joints. They bend and straighten, but cannot make a circle.
terms.art: A door swinging on its hinges next to an arm bending at the elbow, with arrows showing the same back-and-forth swing.

terms.meaning: In a ball and socket joint, the round end of one bone sits in a cup in another bone. It can move in almost every direction.
terms.example: Your shoulder and hip are ball and socket joints. You can swing your straight arm round in a big circle.
terms.art: A round laddu sitting in a small steel cup, next to a drawing of the top of an arm bone sitting in the shoulder.

terms.meaning: A muscle is a soft part of your body that can get shorter and pull. Muscles pull on bones to move them.
terms.example: When you bend your arm to lift a water bottle, the muscle at the front of your upper arm gets short, fat and hard.
terms.art: A girl lifting a filled steel water bottle by bending her arm, with her other hand on the front of her upper arm.

terms.meaning: A tendon is a strong cord that joins a muscle to a bone.
terms.example: Stand on tiptoe and feel the back of your ankle. The hard cord there is a tendon. It joins your calf muscle to your heel bone.
terms.art: A child standing on tiptoe while a grown-up's finger touches the tight cord at the back of the ankle.

terms.meaning: Cartilage is a smooth, bendy material in the body. It is softer than bone.
terms.example: The tip of your nose and the flap of your ear are cartilage. That is why they bend when you press them.
terms.art: A child gently bending the tip of their nose with one finger and folding the top of their ear with the other hand.

terms.meaning: Your skull is the bone of your head. It is a hard case round your brain.
terms.example: Tap gently on the top of your head. You feel your skull under your hair.
terms.art: A child tapping the top of their head with two fingers, with a faint drawing of the skull under the hair.

terms.meaning: Ribs are curved bones round your chest. Together they make a cage that keeps your heart and lungs safe.
terms.example: Put your hands on your sides and breathe in. You can feel your ribs move out and in.
terms.art: A child with both hands on the sides of their chest, with faint curved rib lines drawn under the T-shirt.

terms.meaning: Your backbone is a long row of small bones down the middle of your back. It holds you up and lets you bend.
terms.example: Bend forward and ask a grown-up to run a finger down your back. The row of bumps is your backbone.
terms.art: A child bending forward while a grown-up runs one finger down the row of bumps on the child's back.

terms.meaning: An X-ray is a special kind of light that goes through skin and muscle. Bone stops more of it, so bones show up white on an X-ray picture.
terms.example: When someone falls and hurts their wrist, a doctor takes an X-ray to see if a bone is broken.
terms.art: A grey X-ray picture of a hand with white finger bones, held up against a bright window.

explanations.context: This card is about the hard parts you can feel under your skin.
explanations.definition: Bones are the hard, living parts inside the body. All the bones together make the skeleton.
explanations.description: Press gently on your shin, your knuckles or your head, and you feel something hard. That is bone. A grown-up has about 206 bones. Some are long, like the leg bones. Some are tiny, like the three little bones deep inside each ear.
examples: The longest bone in your body is your thigh bone. It goes from your hip to your knee.
The smallest bone is deep inside your ear. It is smaller than a grain of rice.
Each hand has 27 bones, and each foot has 26.
explanations.art: A child's outline with the main bones drawn faintly inside: skull, ribs, backbone, arm bones and leg bones.

explanations.context: This card is about why a body has a skeleton at all.
explanations.definition: Bones hold the body up, keep soft parts safe, and give muscles something to pull on.
explanations.description: Without bones, you would flop like an empty sock. Your leg bones carry your weight when you stand. Your skull is a hard case round your soft brain. Your ribs make a cage round your heart and lungs. Muscles are joined to bones, and they pull on them to move you.
examples: The skull keeps the brain safe.
The ribs keep the heart and lungs safe.
The backbone holds you up and keeps the soft cord of nerves inside it safe.
Leg bones carry your weight when you walk.
explanations.art: Three small pictures side by side: a skull round a brain, ribs round a heart and lungs, and leg bones holding up a standing child.

explanations.context: This card is about the places where your body bends.
explanations.definition: A joint is a place where two bones meet. Most joints let the body bend or turn.
explanations.description: A bone is stiff. It does not bend. So you can only bend where two bones meet. Each finger has three bones and bends in three places. Smooth cartilage covers the bone ends, and a slippery liquid helps them slide, like oil in a door hinge.
examples: Each finger has 3 bones. The thumb has 2 bones you can feel, and another inside the palm.
Your elbow, knee, wrist, ankle, shoulder and hip are joints.
Your skull is made of many bones that joined together. Those joints do not move.
explanations.art: A close-up drawing of one finger with its three bones shown inside, and small circles at the three joints.

explanations.concept: Hinge joints and ball and socket joints
explanations.context: In the Torch on the Wall experiment, you moved one joint at a time and watched the torch light on the wall. This card explains what you saw.
explanations.definition: A hinge joint moves one way and back, like a door. A ball and socket joint can move in almost every direction, because a round ball of bone turns in a cup.
explanations.description: At your elbow, the bones fit together like a hinge. So in the Torch on the Wall experiment, the torch light could only go up and down in a line. At your shoulder, the round top of your arm bone sits in a shallow cup. So the light could go round in a whole circle. Your knee and the middle joints of your fingers are hinges. Your hip is a ball and socket joint. Your wrist and big knuckles are in between. They can draw a small circle.
examples: Hinge joints: elbow, knee, the middle and end joints of your fingers.
Ball and socket joints: shoulder and hip.
In between: wrist, ankle, and the big knuckles where your fingers join your hand.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: an elbow with an arrow going up and down in a line, and a shoulder with an arrow going round in a circle.

explanations.context: This card is about what moves your bones at a joint.
explanations.definition: Muscles move bones by getting shorter and pulling on them. A muscle can pull, but it cannot push.
explanations.description: Put your hand on the front of your upper arm and bend your elbow. The muscle there gets shorter, fatter and harder. It is pulling your forearm up. To straighten your arm, a muscle at the back of your upper arm pulls instead. Muscles are joined to bones by strong cords called tendons. You have more than 600 muscles.
examples: The muscle at the front of your upper arm bends your elbow.
Your calf muscle pulls your heel up when you stand on tiptoe.
Your heart is a muscle too. It squeezes blood round your body.
explanations.art: An arm bending at the elbow, with the upper arm muscle drawn short and fat, and a tendon joining the muscle to the forearm bone.

explanations.context: This card is about why a broken bone can mend.
explanations.definition: Bone is living. It has living bone cells and blood running through it.
explanations.description: Bone looks hard like stone, but it is alive. Inside are bone cells that build new bone and take away old bone, all through your life. When a bone breaks, the bone cells build new bone across the crack. A doctor puts on a plaster cast only to keep the pieces still, so they join straight. Many bones also make blood inside them, in the soft middle called marrow.
examples: A child's broken arm usually mends in a few weeks.
Bone cells build more bone where your body pushes on it most, for example in a tennis player's hitting arm.
Astronauts in space lose some bone, because nothing presses on their bones there.
explanations.art: Two X-ray pictures of the same arm bone: one with a dark crack across it, and one some weeks later with a slightly thicker white patch where the crack has joined.

explanations.concept: Children have more bones than grown-ups
explanations.context: This card is about how a skeleton changes as you grow.
explanations.definition: A newborn baby has about 300 bones and bits of bone. Many of them join together as the child grows, until a grown-up has about 206.
explanations.description: A baby's skull is made of plates with soft gaps between them. You may have felt the soft spot on a baby's head. The plates join up as the child grows. A baby's kneecaps are soft cartilage, and they slowly turn into bone during the first few years. Bones keep growing longer until the teenage years.
examples: The soft spot on top of a baby's head closes by about the age of 2.
A baby's lower jaw starts as two halves, which join in the first year.
The bones at the bottom of the backbone join together by the time a person is grown up.
explanations.art: A baby lying on a mat with a grown-up's hand gently resting on the top of the baby's head.

explanations.context: This card is about the bones of other animals, including the ones near your home.
explanations.definition: Most fish, and all frogs, lizards, birds and mammals, have a skeleton of bone inside, with a backbone. Humans are one of these animals.
explanations.description: A crow, a cat, a house lizard and you all have a backbone, a skull and ribs. The bones are the same kinds, in different shapes and sizes. A giraffe has 7 bones in her neck, the same number as you, but each one is very long. Ants, spiders and crabs have no bones. Their hard skeleton is on the outside, like a coat of armour.
examples: A giraffe and a human both have 7 neck bones.
A bird's leg seems to bend backwards. That bend is really the ankle. The knee is hidden up in the feathers.
An ant's hard skeleton is on the outside of their body.
explanations.art: A row of skeletons drawn side by side: a human child, a cat, a crow and a fish, with the backbone of each one coloured the same.

agreed.text: A grown-up human has about 206 bones. A newborn baby has more separate pieces, about 300, and many of them join as the child grows.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have counted bones in skeletons and watched them on X-rays of children of every age.

agreed.text: Bones are alive. Bone cells build and remove bone all through life, and a broken bone can mend.
agreed.evidence: X-ray pictures taken weeks apart show new bone growing across a break. Under a microscope, bone is full of living cells and tiny blood tubes.

agreed.text: Muscles move bones by pulling. A muscle cannot push.
agreed.evidence: When a muscle works, you can feel it get shorter and harder. To move a joint back again, a different muscle on the other side pulls.

agreed.text: Most fish, and frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals, including humans, have a backbone and a skeleton of bone inside.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have compared the skeletons of thousands of animals. The same kinds of bones turn up again and again, in different shapes.

challenging.for: Most grown-ups do have 206 bones when doctors count them in the usual way.
challenging.against: Babies have about 300 pieces. Some grown-ups have an extra rib, or extra small bones in the hands and feet. Old Indian books counted differently: the Sushruta Samhita counts 300 bones and the Charaka Samhita 360, because they counted teeth, nails and some cartilage too.
challenging.context: This card is about how many bones a person really has.

challenging.claim: Cracking your knuckles gives you joint illness when you are old.
challenging.for: The popping sound is loud, and it seems as if something must be getting hurt.
challenging.against: A doctor named Donald Unger cracked the knuckles of only his left hand for about 60 years. When he checked, both hands were just as healthy. Larger studies have found no clear link either.
challenging.context: This card is about the popping sound some people make with their fingers.

challenging.claim: The pop when you crack a knuckle is a bubble forming in the joint liquid.
challenging.who: Some scientists who filmed knuckles cracking inside a scanner, in 2015
challenging.for: Their pictures showed a gap of gas appearing in the joint liquid at the moment of the pop.
challenging.against: Earlier scientists, and some who made computer models later, said the sound comes from a bubble collapsing, partly or fully.
challenging.context: This card is about what really makes the popping sound.

challenging.claim: Bones are dead, like stones, once they have finished growing.
challenging.who: A common idea, because a skeleton looks hard and dry
challenging.for: The bones you see in a museum are hard and dry, and they do not change.
challenging.against: Bones in a living body have blood and living cells. They mend when broken and get thicker when used more.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the bones inside you are living.

big_questions.q: Your bones are made from the food you ate. When does the food stop being food and start being you?
big_questions.hint: Think of the milk, ragi and greens you ate last week. Where are they now?

big_questions.q: A bone is stiff, but your body bends. How can a body made of stiff parts be so bendy?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many places your finger bends, and what is at each one.

big_questions.q: Why would a body need some joints that move only one way?
big_questions.hint: Think of standing on one leg. Would you want your knee to swing round in every direction?

big_questions.q: Bone cells build more bone where your body is pushed the most. How do you think they can tell where that is?
big_questions.hint: Scientists know part of the answer. Bone cells sense pushes and send signals to each other.

story.title: Thatha's Wrist and the Picture of Bones
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that bones show up white on an X-ray, that bones are alive, and that a broken bone mends when it is kept still.
text: Revathi lived with her Amma and her Thatha in a flat on the third floor in Madurai. Thatha was her grandfather. Every morning he made filter coffee. He poured it from the tumbler to the davara and back again, high in the air, to make it frothy.

One Monday the bathroom floor was wet. Thatha slipped. He put out his right hand to stop his fall, and he landed hard on his wrist. "Aiyo!" he cried. His wrist began to swell, and it hurt when he tried to turn his hand.

Amma called an auto, and the three of them went to the hospital. A doctor with grey hair and kind eyes looked at Thatha's wrist. Her name was Dr Fathima. "We need to see inside," she said. "We will take an X-ray."
"What is an X-ray?" Revathi asked.
"It is a special kind of light that goes through skin and muscle," said Dr Fathima. "Bone stops more of it. So on the X-ray picture, the bones show up white."
A nurse named Selvi asked Thatha to rest his hand flat on a table and keep very still. Then she took the picture. Later, Dr Fathima held a large grey sheet up against the bright window.

Revathi gasped. There was Thatha's hand. But it was a hand made of white bones! Each finger had a row of long thin bones. Near the wrist was a bunch of small round bones, packed together like pebbles in a bag.
"Look here," said Dr Fathima. She pointed to a thin dark line across a bone just above the wrist. "This bone has a crack. It is broken."
Thatha sighed. "Then my wrist is finished," he said. "A bone is like a stone. When a stone cracks, it stays cracked."

Dr Fathima smiled. "A stone is not alive, Sir. Your bone is. Inside it there are living bone cells, and blood runs through it. The bone cells will build new bone across the crack. Our job is only to hold the pieces still, so they join straight."

Nurse Selvi wrapped Thatha's arm in a hard white plaster cast. It went from his knuckles almost to his elbow. "Can you wiggle your fingers?" asked Dr Fathima. Thatha wiggled them. "Can you bend your elbow?" He bent it. "Can you bend your wrist?" He tried, but the cast held it straight.
"Why can he move his fingers but not his wrist?" asked Revathi.
"Because you bend only where two bones meet," said Dr Fathima. "Those places are called joints. The cast covers the wrist joint, so it keeps it still. The finger joints are outside the cast."

At home, Revathi sat beside Thatha on the sofa and looked at her own hand. She bent one finger slowly. It bent in three places. "Thatha, my finger has three bones, like the white ones in your picture!" She bent her thumb. It bent in two places. "And my thumb has two."
"How do you know they are bones?" asked Thatha.

Revathi pressed the back of her finger. "Feel. It is hard inside, between the bends. And it bends only at the joints." Thatha pressed her finger with his good hand. "You are right," he said. "I have had this hand for seventy years, and I never counted."

Every day for six weeks, Thatha drank his milk and ate his ragi kali and keerai. Dr Fathima had said that bone cells need good food to build new bone. Revathi drew a calendar and crossed off each day with a red pencil.

Then they went back to the hospital. Nurse Selvi took a new X-ray. This time the dark line was gone. In its place was a slightly thicker white patch on the bone. "The bone cells have done their work," said Dr Fathima. "The crack is filled with new bone."

The cast came off. Thatha's wrist was stiff, and his arm looked thin, because he had not used it for weeks. "Move it gently every day," said Dr Fathima. "Bones and muscles grow stronger when you use them."
A week later, Thatha made filter coffee again. He poured it from the tumbler to the davara, not quite as high as before. Revathi watched his wrist turn. "Your bone mended itself, Thatha," she said.
Thatha laughed. "My doctor and my granddaughter have taught an old man two things," he said. "Bones are not stones. They are alive. And I bend only where my bones meet."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Thatha thinks a bone is like a stone, so a cracked bone stays cracked. The X-ray and the doctor show that bone is alive and builds new bone across a crack. Revathi also finds, by bending her own finger, that a body bends only at its joints.
ask: Why do bones show up white on an X-ray picture?
Why did Thatha think his wrist would stay broken?
What was the plaster cast for, if the bone cells did the mending?
Why could Thatha wiggle his fingers in the cast but not bend his wrist?

A woman doctor with grey hair holding a grey X-ray of a hand up against a bright hospital window, while a girl stares at the white bones.

experiments.title: Torch on the Wall: which joints can draw a circle?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hold a torch and move only one joint at a time. The light on the wall shows how that joint can move. Some joints make the light go round in a circle. Some make it go only up and down in a line.
experiments.question: If you move only one joint, which joints can make the torch light draw a whole circle on the wall, and which can only make it go back and forth in a line?
experiments.predict: Guess first, for each joint: shoulder, elbow, wrist, the big knuckle of your finger, and the middle joint of your finger. Will it draw a circle or only a line? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Only one joint moves each time, so we know which joint made the shape. A grown-up gently holds the part above the joint still. You stand at the same spot each time. You try each joint three times, because one try can be a mistake.

materials.item: a torch, or a grown-up's phone with the torch switched on
a room you can make dark, with a plain wall
a table or a bed edge to rest your arm on
a sketch pen, to put a small dot on your fingernail
a pencil and the results table on paper

schedule.what: Guess for each joint, then test each one with the torch, fill in the table, and talk about why.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Next to each joint, draw the shape the light made: a circle or a line.

setup.art: A dark bedroom with the curtains closed and a plain wall, a torch on the bed, and a girl standing about two big steps from the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dark. Stand two big steps from a plain wall.

setup.art: A girl holding a lit torch in her fist with her arm straight out like a stick, and a big circle of light drawn on the wall in a dotted line.
setup.caption: 2. Shoulder: keep your arm straight and move only at the shoulder.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a girl's upper arm against her side, while the girl moves only her forearm and the torch light goes up and down the wall in a line.
setup.caption: 3. Elbow: a grown-up holds your upper arm still. Move only your forearm.

setup.art: A girl resting her forearm flat on a table edge, with her hand and the torch sticking out past the edge, moving only at the wrist.
setup.caption: 4. Wrist: rest your forearm on a table. Move only your hand.

setup.art: A child's hand flat on a table with one finger lifted, a small sketch-pen dot on the fingernail, and a dotted path in the air above it.
setup.caption: 5. Finger joints: hold the hand flat and watch the fingertip.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table on paper with five rows: shoulder, elbow, wrist, big knuckle, middle finger joint. 2. Ask your child to guess for each joint, and to give a reason. 3. Write each guess in the table.
flow.say: We will hold a torch and move only one joint at a time. For each joint, will the light draw a circle or only a line? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each joint. Will the light draw a circle, or a line? Why?

good: The shoulder can go round, because I can swing my arm.
The elbow only bends, so it will make a line.
All of them can make circles, because I can move my arm round.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as there is a reason. Do not tell your child the answers. Many children guess that the elbow can draw a circle.

flow.do: 1. Close the curtains and switch off the lights. 2. Your child stands about two big steps from a plain wall. 3. Switch the torch on and give it to your child.
flow.say: This is our wall. Point the torch at it. Can you see the spot of light?
flow.kid: Stand two big steps from the wall. Point the torch at it.
flow.parent: Evening is easiest. If you use your phone, stay close and hold your child's wrist lightly so the phone is not dropped.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the torch in a fist, with the arm straight like a stick. 2. They keep the elbow and wrist straight. 3. They move only at the shoulder, and try to make the light go round in a circle. 4. Try three times.
flow.say: Keep your arm straight like a stick. Move only at your shoulder. Can you make the light go round in a circle?
flow.kid: Keep your arm straight. Move only your shoulder. Can the light go round?
flow.parent: The light usually goes round in a big circle. Write what you saw in the table.

flow.do: 1. Hold your child's upper arm gently against their side, so it cannot move. 2. Your child moves only the forearm, from the elbow. 3. Ask them to try to make a circle. 4. Try three times.
flow.say: I am holding your upper arm still. Now move only your elbow. Try hard to make a circle. What does the light do?
flow.kid: Keep your upper arm still. Move only your elbow. Try to make a circle.

good: It only went up and down.
It made a line, not a circle.
I could not make it go round.

flow.parent: The light goes up and down in a line or a curve. Your child may twist the forearm. That turns the torch, but the spot hardly moves round. The twist happens where the two forearm bones roll over each other.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests the forearm flat on a table or a bed edge, with the hand and torch past the edge. 2. Press the forearm gently down. 3. Your child moves only the hand, at the wrist. 4. Try three times.
flow.say: Your arm stays on the table. Move only your wrist. Can the light go round?
flow.kid: Keep your arm on the table. Move only your wrist. Can the light go round?
flow.parent: The wrist can usually draw a small circle or an oval. It moves up and down and side to side. It is in between a hinge joint and a ball and socket joint.

flow.do: 1. Put a small sketch-pen dot on the nail of your child's pointing finger. 2. Your child lays the hand flat on the table and you hold the back of the hand down. 3. First they lift the finger from the big knuckle and try to draw a circle in the air. 4. Then you hold the finger below the middle joint, and they move only the top part.
flow.say: Watch the dot on your nail. First move only the big knuckle. Can the dot go round? Now I hold your finger. Move only the top part. Can it go round now?
flow.kid: Watch the dot on your nail. Can it go round? Now try with only the top part.
flow.parent: The big knuckle can usually draw a small circle. The middle joint can only bend and straighten, so the dot goes back and forth. Put both results in the table.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which joints drew a circle? Which only drew a line? Why do you think the shoulder and the elbow are so different?
flow.kid: Which joints made a circle? Which made a line? Why are they different?

ask.q: Why can the shoulder draw a circle when the elbow cannot?
good: The bones fit together in a different shape.
The shoulder is round, so it turns every way.
The elbow is like a door. It only opens and shuts.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the table: 'My shoulder made a circle, but my elbow only made a line.' Then read the card on hinge joints and ball and socket joints.

check.q: You hold a torch and move only your elbow. What does the light on the wall do?
options: It goes up and down in a line
It goes round in a big circle
It does not move at all
check.why: The elbow is a hinge joint. It bends and straightens like a door, so the light goes back and forth in a line. If you picked the circle, try your elbow again with a grown-up holding your upper arm still.

experiments.title: Bone Hunt: where is bone close to your skin?
experiments.context: In this experiment you press gently on different parts of your body. You find out where you can feel hard bone just under the skin, and where you feel only soft parts.
experiments.question: On which parts of your body can you feel hard bone just under the skin, and on which parts can you feel only soft muscle and fat?
experiments.predict: Look at the list of 14 places. For each one, guess: will you feel hard bone, or only soft parts? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You press every place the same way: gently, with two fingertips. You press each place on a grown-up too, to see if bodies are the same. You only count it as bone if it feels hard and does not squash.
results_table: What I felt on a grown-up

materials.item: a big sheet of paper or newspaper with an outline of a body drawn on it
a red and a blue crayon or sketch pen
the list of 14 places, written on paper

schedule.what: Guess for each place, then press gently on yourself and a grown-up, colour the body outline, and count the results.

experiments.record: Colour the body outline: a red dot where you felt hard bone, a blue dot where you felt only soft parts. Count the red dots and the blue dots.

setup.art: A simple outline of a child's body drawn on a sheet of newspaper, with a red and a blue sketch pen beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a body outline on paper.

setup.art: A child pressing two fingertips gently on the front of their lower leg, then on their tummy.
setup.caption: 2. Press gently with two fingertips. Is it hard or soft?

setup.art: The body outline with red dots on the head, collarbone, elbow, knee and ankle, and blue dots on the tummy, upper arm and calf.
setup.caption: 3. Red dot for hard bone, blue dot for soft.

flow.do: 1. Draw a simple body outline on paper. 2. Read out the 14 places on the list. 3. Ask your child to guess hard or soft for each one, with a reason.
flow.say: We will hunt for bones by pressing gently. Will the tip of your nose be hard or soft? What about your tummy? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each place. Hard bone, or soft? Why?
flow.parent: The 14 places are: top of the head, forehead, top of the nose, tip of the nose, ear flap, collarbone, sides of the chest, front of the tummy, point of the elbow, middle of the upper arm, kneecap, front of the shin, back of the calf, and the knobs at the ankle. Write the guesses in the table. Do not say the answers yet.

flow.do: Your child presses each place gently with two fingertips, one at a time. After each one, they put a red or a blue dot on the body outline.
flow.say: Press gently, like you are feeling a ripe mango. If it is hard and does not squash, it is bone. Put a red dot. If it is soft, put a blue dot.
flow.kid: Press gently with two fingers. If it is hard, put a red dot. If it is soft, put a blue dot.

good: The tip of my nose bends!
My tummy has no bone at the front.
My ear is bendy, not hard.

flow.parent: Hard bone is easy to feel on the head, the top of the nose, the collarbone, the ribs, the elbow, the kneecap, the shin and the ankle knobs. The tummy and the middle of the upper arm and calf feel soft. The nose tip and the ear flap bend, because they are cartilage, not bone. Press gently on the chest and tummy, never hard.

flow.do: Your child presses the same places on you. Talk about whether your body felt the same.
flow.say: Now press on me, gently. Is my body the same as yours?
flow.kid: Now press on the grown-up, gently. Is it the same as you?
flow.parent: The bones are in the same places on everyone. On a grown-up some may be harder to feel, because there is more muscle or fat over them.

flow.do: Count the red dots and the blue dots. Talk about what you found.
flow.say: How many red dots? How many blue dots? Why do you think there is bone over your chest but not over your tummy?
flow.kid: Count the red dots and the blue dots. Why is there no bone on your tummy?

ask.q: Why is there bone over your chest but not at the front of your tummy?
good: The ribs keep my heart and lungs safe.
My tummy has to bend and get bigger after I eat.

flow.parent: Most children find about 9 or 10 red places and 4 or 5 blue ones. There is bone at the back of the tummy: the backbone. The front needs to bend and stretch when you bend over, breathe and eat.

check.q: You press the tip of your nose and it bends. Why?
options: The tip of the nose is cartilage, which is bendy
There is a bone there, but it is soft
check.why: The top of the nose is bone, but the tip is cartilage. Cartilage is smooth and bendy, softer than bone. If you picked another answer, press the top of your nose and then the tip, and feel the difference.

activities.title: Bend and Dot: how many bones are in your hand?
activities.context: In this activity you bend each finger slowly and put a dot where it bends. Between the dots are bones. You count the bones in your fingers and thumb.

materials.item: a washable sketch pen
a sheet of paper to draw round your hand

schedule.what: Bend each finger, dot the bends, count the bones, and draw round your hand.

activities.record: Draw round your hand on paper. Draw the bones inside each finger as short lines, and the joints as dots.

setup.art: A child's hand with the pointing finger bent slowly, and a grown-up drawing a small dot on the back of the finger at each bend.
setup.caption: 1. Bend one finger slowly. Put a dot where it bends.

setup.art: A hand outline on paper with three short lines inside each finger and two inside the thumb, and dots between them.
setup.caption: 2. Draw round your hand. Draw a line for each bone.

flow.do: Ask your child to bend one finger very slowly and watch where it bends.
flow.say: Bend your pointing finger very slowly. Where does it bend? How many places? Why do you think it bends there and not everywhere?
flow.kid: Bend one finger very slowly. Where does it bend? How many places?
flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Let your child notice that the finger bends in only a few places.

flow.do: 1. Put a small sketch-pen dot on the back of the finger at each bend, including the big knuckle. 2. Do the same for every finger and the thumb. 3. Press between the dots.
flow.say: Let's put a dot at every bend. Now press between the dots. Is it hard or soft in there?
flow.kid: Put a dot at every bend. Press between the dots. Hard or soft?
flow.parent: Each finger bends in three places, so it has three bones. The thumb bends in two places that are easy to see, so it has two bones in the thumb part. Its third long bone is inside the palm.

flow.do: Draw round your child's hand on paper. Your child draws the bones and joints inside, and counts the finger bones.
flow.say: Draw a short line for each bone, and a dot for each joint. How many bones are in your four fingers and thumb altogether?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each bone. Count them all. How many?
flow.parent: Four fingers with 3 bones each make 12. The thumb adds 2. That makes 14 bones in the fingers and thumb of one hand. The whole hand, with the palm and the wrist, has 27 bones.

check.q: You bend your middle finger slowly and count three bends. How many bones are in that finger?
check.why: A finger bends only where two bones meet. Three bends, counting the big knuckle, means three bones. If you picked 1, press between the dots on your own finger and feel the hard parts.

activities.title: Floppy Sock Arm: why do we need bones?
activities.context: In this activity you make a model arm from an old sock. You see what an arm would do with no bone, with one long bone, and with two bones and a joint.

materials.item: an old long sock
a 30-centimetre ruler, or a stick about that long
two pencils or two short sticks

schedule.what: Hold up the sock with nothing inside, with a ruler inside, and with two pencils inside, and see what each one can do.

activities.record: Draw the three socks: floppy, stiff, and bending in the middle.

setup.art: An empty sock held up by one end, flopping down.
setup.caption: 1. An empty sock flops down.

setup.art: A sock with a ruler inside, standing out straight from a child's hand.
setup.caption: 2. With a ruler inside, it stays straight but cannot bend.

setup.art: A sock with two pencils inside end to end, bending in the middle where the pencils meet.
setup.caption: 3. With two pencils, it bends where they meet.

flow.do: Hold the empty sock up by its open end, so it hangs down. Then hold it out sideways.
flow.say: This sock is an arm with no bones. Can it point at the door? Why not?
flow.kid: This sock has no bones. Can it point at the door?
flow.parent: The sock flops. Nothing inside holds it up.

flow.do: Push the ruler into the sock and hold it out sideways again. Then try to bend it.
flow.say: Now it has one long bone. Can it point? Can it bend to scratch your nose?
flow.kid: Now it has one long bone. Can it point? Can it bend?
flow.parent: It points, but it cannot bend at all.

flow.do: Take out the ruler. Push in two pencils, one after the other, so they meet in the middle of the sock. Bend the sock where they meet.
flow.say: Now it has two bones and a joint between them. What can it do now? Which part of your own arm is like this?
flow.kid: Now it has two bones. Bend it where they meet. Which part of you is like this?

ask.q: Which part of your body is like the sock with two pencils?
good: My elbow. It bends in the middle of my arm.
My finger. It has bones and bends between them.

flow.parent: A body needs both: stiff bones to hold it up, and joints so it can bend. In a real arm, muscles do the bending.

activities.title: Muscle Feel: what does a muscle do when it works?
activities.context: In this activity you put your hand on a muscle while you lift something. You feel the muscle change shape. Then you find a tendon, the cord that joins a muscle to a bone.

materials.item: a steel or plastic water bottle filled with water, about half a litre or 1 litre

schedule.what: Feel the upper arm muscle while lifting a bottle, then feel the heel tendon while standing on tiptoe.

activities.record: Draw your arm twice: once straight, with a long thin muscle, and once bent, with a short fat muscle.

setup.art: A girl holding a filled steel water bottle with her arm straight down, her other hand resting on the front of her upper arm.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a bottle with your arm straight. Feel the front of your upper arm.

setup.art: The same girl bending her elbow to lift the bottle up to her shoulder, her other hand feeling the muscle bulge.
setup.caption: 2. Bend your arm to lift the bottle. Feel the muscle change.

setup.art: A child standing on tiptoe holding the back of a chair, with a finger on the cord at the back of the ankle.
setup.caption: 3. Stand on tiptoe. Feel the cord above your heel.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the bottle with the arm hanging straight. 2. They rest the other hand on the front of the upper arm. 3. They slowly bend the elbow and lift the bottle up, then slowly put it down.
flow.say: Feel the front of your upper arm. Now lift the bottle slowly. What happens under your hand? What happens when you put it down?
flow.kid: Feel your upper arm. Lift the bottle slowly. What changes under your hand?

good: It got hard and fat.
It went up into a bump.
It got short when I lifted.

flow.parent: The muscle gets shorter, fatter and harder as it pulls the forearm up. When the arm goes down, it gets long and soft again.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds a chair and stands on tiptoe. 2. They feel the back of the ankle, just above the heel. 3. They go up and down a few times.
flow.say: Stand on tiptoe. Feel just above your heel at the back. What is that hard cord? What happens to it when you go up?
flow.kid: Stand on tiptoe. Feel above your heel at the back. What is that cord?
flow.parent: This is a tendon. It joins the big calf muscle to the heel bone. When the calf muscle pulls, the tendon pulls the heel up.

check.q: You lift a bottle and feel the muscle in your upper arm get short and hard. What is the muscle doing?
options: Pulling on a bone to bend your arm
check.why: Muscles move bones by getting shorter and pulling. They cannot push. If you picked pushing, try again with your hand on the muscle and feel it get shorter as you lift.

activities.title: Backward Knees? Look at a bird's leg
activities.context: In this activity you look at how a bird's leg bends, at your window or in a picture. Then you find the same joints in your own leg. A bird's leg seems to bend backwards, but that bend is really the ankle.

materials.item: a crow, pigeon or myna at your window or balcony, or a clear picture of a bird standing
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Watch a bird's leg, then stand on tiptoe and compare your own leg.

activities.record: Draw a bird's leg and your leg on tiptoe side by side. Label the knee, the ankle and the toes on both.

setup.art: A crow standing on a balcony railing, with a circle round the bend in the leg that points backwards.
setup.caption: 1. Look at where a bird's leg bends.

setup.art: A child standing on tiptoe next to a drawing of a crow's leg, with the ankle and heel of both circled in the same colour.
setup.caption: 2. Stand on tiptoe. Your heel is up, like the bird's.

flow.do: Watch a bird at the window, or look at a picture. Point to the bend halfway down the bird's leg.
flow.say: Look at the crow's leg. Which way does the bend in the middle point? Is it like your knee? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the bird's leg. Which way does it bend? Is it like your knee?
flow.parent: If no bird comes, a clear photo from a book or the internet works. The bend points backwards, the opposite way to a human knee.

flow.do: Your child stands on tiptoe, holding a chair. Point to their heel, which is now up off the floor.
flow.say: Stand on tiptoe. Look at your heel. Which way does your ankle bend now? Does it look like the bird's leg?
flow.kid: Stand on tiptoe. Look at your heel. Does it look like the bird's leg?
flow.parent: A bird stands on their toes all the time. The bend that looks like a backward knee is really the ankle. The bird's knee is higher up, hidden in the feathers, and bends forward like yours.

flow.do: Draw the two legs side by side and label them.
flow.say: Let's draw the bird's leg and your tiptoe leg. Where is the knee on each? Where is the ankle?
flow.kid: Draw both legs. Mark the knee and the ankle on each.

check.q: The bend in a crow's leg that points backwards is really which joint?
check.why: Birds walk on their toes, with the heel up. The backward bend is the ankle. The knee is hidden in the feathers higher up. If you picked the knee, stand on tiptoe again and look at where your heel is.

games.title: Bone, Bend or Soft?
games.context: This is a game about your own body. Each card names a place on the body. Players guess if it is hard bone, a joint that bends, or soft. Then everyone checks on their own body.

printables.title: 16 cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: The front of your leg, below the knee
items.b: Bone. This is your shin bone, just under the skin.
Bend. The elbow is a hinge joint. It bends one way, like a door.
Soft. There is no bone at the front of the tummy, so it can bend and stretch.
Bone. Your skull is a hard case round your brain.
Soft and bendy. It is cartilage, not bone.
Bend. The shoulder is a ball and socket joint. It moves in a circle.
Bone. These are your ribs. They keep your heart and lungs safe.

items.f: The back of your lower leg, the calf
items.b: Soft. This is a big muscle. The bone is deep inside it.
Bend. The knee is a hinge joint.
Soft and bendy. It is cartilage, not bone.

items.f: The bumps down the middle of your back
items.b: Bone. These are the small bones of your backbone.
Bend. The wrist moves up and down and side to side.

items.f: The bone that runs across the top of your chest to your shoulder
items.b: Bone. This is your collarbone.

items.f: The middle of your upper arm
items.b: Soft on the outside. It is muscle. The bone is deep inside.

items.f: The knobs on each side of your ankle
items.b: Bone. These are the ends of your leg bones.
Bend. The hip is a ball and socket joint, like the shoulder.

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player reads the top card aloud.
Everyone shows an answer at the same time: a fist for bone, a bending finger for a joint that bends, an open soft hand for soft.
Everyone checks on their own body by pressing gently or bending. Then turn the card over and read the back aloud.
Everyone with the right answer gets one point. Take turns reading. When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. If two players have the same points, they share the win.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards cut from paper in a face-down pile on a mat, with three children sitting round them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and put them face down.

setup.art: Three hand signs drawn side by side: a fist, a bending finger, and an open soft hand.
setup.caption: 2. Fist for bone, bending finger for a joint, open hand for soft.

setup.art: A girl pressing the tip of her nose with one finger while holding a card in her other hand.
setup.caption: 3. Check on your own body, then turn the card over.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Show the three hand signs.
flow.say: A fist means bone. A bending finger means a joint. An open soft hand means soft.
flow.kid: Fist means bone. Bending finger means joint. Open hand means soft.

flow.do: Take turns reading the cards. Everyone shows a sign, then checks on their own body, then reads the back.
flow.say: This card says: the tip of your nose. Show me your sign! Now press it gently. Were you right?
flow.kid: Read a card. Show your sign. Check on your body. Read the back.

good: My nose tip is not bone!
My tummy has no bone at the front.
My calf is soft but there is bone inside.

flow.parent: Let your child press each place before turning the card. Feeling it is the point of the game.

flow.do: Count the points and talk.
flow.say: Count the points. Which card fooled the most players? Why?
flow.kid: Count the points. Which card fooled the most players?

check.q: Which of these is a joint?
check.why: A joint is where two bones meet, and the knee is where the thigh bone meets the shin bone. The shin is one bone, and the nose tip is cartilage. If you picked another, bend your knee and feel where it bends.

games.title: Build a Skeleton: a bone card race
games.context: This is a building game. Each player builds a skeleton on the floor from bone cards. To keep a card, you must answer the question on it.

printables.title: 12 bone cards to cut out, with a question on the back (print the page once for each player)

items.b: Question: what does your skull keep safe? Answer: your brain.
Question: where can you feel your backbone? Answer: the row of bumps down the middle of your back.
Question: what do your ribs keep safe? Answer: your heart and lungs.
Question: where are your collarbones? Answer: across the top of your chest, out to your shoulders.
Question: is the shoulder a hinge or a ball and socket joint? Answer: a ball and socket joint.
Question: which joint is between the upper arm and the forearm? Answer: the elbow.
Question: how many bones are in one finger? Answer: 3.
Question: name a ball and socket joint in your leg. Answer: the hip.
Question: which is the longest bone in your body? Answer: the thigh bone.
Question: is a baby's kneecap hard bone? Answer: no, it is soft cartilage at first and turns to bone over a few years.
Question: can your knee make a circle? Answer: no, it is a hinge joint. It bends one way and back.
Question: what joins your calf muscle to your heel bone? Answer: a tendon.

rules: Print the page once for each player, so everyone has a set of 12 bone cards. Mix your set and put it face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card from your own pile. The player next to you reads the question on the back.
If you answer right, put the bone in the right place on the floor in your skeleton. If not, put the card at the bottom of your pile.
The first player to finish a whole skeleton, with every bone in the right place, wins.

setup.art: Twelve bone cards cut out and spread on the floor: a skull, ribs, backbone, arm and leg bones, hands and feet.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out one set of 12 cards for each player.

setup.art: Two children on a floor, each building a skeleton from bone cards, one placing the thigh bone card below the hip card.
setup.caption: 2. Answer the question, then put the bone in its place.

flow.do: Cut out one set of cards for each player. Each player clears a space on the floor.
flow.say: You will build a skeleton on the floor, bone by bone. Where will the skull go?
flow.kid: You will build a skeleton on the floor. Where does the skull go?

flow.do: Play the game. Help place the bones in the right spots if needed.
flow.say: Your card is the thigh bone. Here is your question. Which is the longest bone in your body?
flow.kid: Take a card. Answer the question. Put the bone in its place.

ask.q: Where does the thigh bone go?
good: Between the hip and the knee.
In the top part of the leg.

flow.parent: Let your child touch the same bone on their own body each time they place a card.

flow.do: Look at the finished skeletons together.
flow.say: Point to every joint in your skeleton. Which ones are hinges? Which are ball and socket joints?
flow.kid: Point to each joint. Which are hinges? Which are ball and socket joints?

check.q: In the Build a Skeleton game, a player puts the thigh bone between the hip and the knee. Is that right?
options: Yes, the thigh bone goes from the hip to the knee
No, it goes in the arm
No, it goes in the foot
check.why: The thigh bone is the long bone at the top of your leg, from your hip joint down to your knee joint. If you picked another answer, put your hands on your hip and your knee, and feel the long bone between them.

projects.title: My Life-Size Bone Map
projects.context: In this project a grown-up draws round you on big paper. You draw your own skeleton inside, feeling each bone on your own body first. You measure your longest bones with string.

materials.item: old newspapers taped together, about as long as your child
a marker or crayon
a piece of string or wool, and a ruler or tailor's tape
cellotape

schedule.what: Lie down on the paper and get drawn round. Feel and draw the skull, ribs, backbone and arm bones.
Feel and draw the hip, leg and foot bones, mark the joints, and measure the longest bones with string.

projects.record: The finished bone map, with every joint circled, and the string lengths of your upper arm, forearm, thigh and shin written beside them.

setup.art: A child lying on newspapers taped together on the floor, while a grown-up draws round them with a marker.
setup.caption: 1. Lie down on the paper. A grown-up draws round you.

setup.art: The outline on the floor with a skull, ribs and a backbone drawn inside, and the child pressing their own ribs before drawing.
setup.caption: 2. Feel each bone on your body, then draw it.

setup.art: A child holding a piece of string from their hip to their knee, while a grown-up marks the string with a pen.
setup.caption: 3. Measure your thigh bone with string.

flow.do: 1. Tape newspapers together on the floor. 2. Your child lies flat on them with arms a little out. 3. Draw round them with a marker.
flow.say: Lie very still, like a starfish. I will draw round you. What do you think is inside this outline?
flow.kid: Lie still like a starfish. A grown-up draws round you.

flow.do: Your child feels each bone on their own body, then draws it inside the outline. Start with the skull, collarbones, ribs, backbone, arm bones and hands.
flow.say: Feel your ribs first. How many can you count on one side? Now draw them.
flow.kid: Feel your ribs. Count them. Now draw them.
flow.parent: Most people have 12 ribs on each side, but a child may count fewer, because the lowest ones are hard to feel. The forearm has two bones side by side.

flow.do: Your child feels and draws the hip bone, thigh bone, kneecap, the two shin bones and the feet. Then they circle every joint.
flow.say: Now the legs. Where is your hip joint? Your knee? Your ankle? Circle each one.
flow.kid: Draw your leg bones. Circle every joint.

good: Shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, ankle.
And the fingers and toes.

flow.do: Hold a string from the hip joint to the knee, then from the knee to the ankle knob. Do the same on the arm. Measure each string with a ruler.
flow.say: Which do you think is longer, your thigh bone or your upper arm bone? Why? Let's measure with string.
flow.kid: Which is longer, your thigh bone or your arm bone? Measure with string.
flow.parent: These string lengths are rough, because you are measuring over skin. The thigh bone should come out longest. It is about one quarter of a person's height.

check.q: You measure your bones with string. Which one is most likely the longest?
check.why: The thigh bone is the longest bone in the body. If your string showed something else, measure again from the hip joint to the knee joint.

challenges.title: Make a Paper Finger That Bends
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Your finger has bones, joints, and tendons that muscles pull. Your job is to make a paper finger that bends when you pull a thread.
challenges.problem: Can you make a paper finger with three bones and three joints, which curls up when you pull a thread, like a real finger?
constraints: Use only paper or card, tape, thread or wool, and scissors.
The finger must bend only at the joints, not in the middle of a bone.
Pulling one thread must make it curl.
materials: a strip of thin card from an old box or greeting card, about 2 centimetres wide and 15 centimetres long
scissors, used by a grown-up or with a grown-up
a pencil, to roll small paper tubes
general: Fold the card lightly in two places to make joints, so it has three bones.
Roll three short paper tubes round a pencil and tape one on each bone, on the same side.
Pass the thread through all three tubes, and tape the end to the tip of the finger. Pull the thread, and the finger curls.
creative: Make a whole hand of five fingers, each with its own thread, and pull them all to make a fist.
Add a second thread on the back of the finger, so you can pull it straight again, the way a second muscle does.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own finger. Does it bend only at the joints? If it bends in the wrong place, what can you change? Try again.

setup.art: A strip of card with two light fold lines across it, making three equal parts.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a card strip lightly in two places.

setup.art: Three small rolled paper tubes taped on the strip, one on each part, with a thread running through them and taped at the tip.
setup.caption: 2. Tape on three paper tubes and thread a string through.

setup.art: A child pulling the thread, and the card finger curling up at the two folds.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the thread. The finger curls.

flow.do: Read the challenge with your child. Let them bend their own finger and feel the back of the hand.
flow.say: When you bend your finger, something pulls it. What do you think pulls it? How could we make a paper finger do the same?
flow.kid: What pulls your finger to bend it? How can paper do the same?

flow.do: Your child builds the finger. A grown-up helps cut the card and tubes.
flow.say: Make your finger. Where will the joints go? What will the thread be?
flow.kid: Build your finger. Fold the card to make joints. The thread is your tendon.
flow.parent: Use scissors with care. If the tubes are taped across the folds, the finger will not bend, so leave the folds clear.

flow.do: Test the finger and improve it.
flow.say: Pull the thread. Does it curl? Does it bend only at the joints? What would make it better?
flow.kid: Pull the thread. Does it curl? What can you change?

check.q: In the paper finger, what does the thread stand for?
options: A tendon, pulled by a muscle
check.why: In a real finger, muscles in your forearm pull on tendons, and the tendons pull the finger bones so the finger curls. The thread does the same job. If you picked bone, look at which part of your model is stiff.

items.p: Label the skeleton: skull, ribs, backbone, thigh bone.
a: skull: the bone of the head
ribs: the curved bones round the chest
backbone: the row of small bones down the back
thigh bone: the long bone from the hip to the knee
items.why: These are four of the biggest parts of the skeleton. A strong answer puts each label on the right part.
items.art: A simple front view of a human skeleton with four empty label lines pointing to the head, the chest, the middle of the back and the top of the leg.

items.p: Draw a line from each bone to the job it does.
pairs: keep the heart and lungs safe
carry your weight when you stand
holds you up and lets you bend
items.why: Bones hold the body up and keep soft parts safe. The skull is a case for the brain, and the ribs are a cage round the heart and lungs.
items.art: Four bones on the left and four small pictures of their jobs on the right, mixed up.

items.p: True or false: the bones inside you are alive.
items.why: True. Bones have living cells and blood inside them. That is why a broken bone can mend.

items.p: Remember the Bend and Dot activity. Draw one of your fingers. Put a dot at every place it bends.
items.a: A finger with three dots: at the big knuckle, the middle and near the tip.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three bends and three bones between them, because a finger bends only where bones meet.
items.art: An empty box with a faint outline of a hand.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why does your finger bend in some places and not in others?
items.a: A bone is stiff. My finger bends only at the joints, where two bones meet.
items.why: A strong answer says that bones do not bend, and that bending happens at joints, between the bones.

items.p: Remember the Bone Hunt. Sort these places into hard bone near the skin, and soft.
items.why: The shin bone and kneecap are just under the skin. The tummy has no bone at the front, and the calf is a thick muscle with the bone deep inside.

items.p: A place where two bones meet is called a ___.
items.why: A joint is where two bones meet. Most joints let you bend or turn.

items.p: In the Torch on the Wall experiment, what did the light on the wall do when you moved only your elbow? Draw the shape it made.
items.a: A straight or curved line going up and down, not a circle.
items.why: The elbow is a hinge joint, like a door. It moves one way and back, so the light makes a line.
items.art: An empty box shaped like a wall, with a small torch drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Which one is not a joint? Elbow, knee, shin, wrist.
items.why: The shin is a bone. The elbow, knee and wrist are joints, the places where two bones meet.

items.p: True or false: a crow has a backbone, like you.
items.why: True. Birds, cats, fish and humans all have a skull, a backbone and ribs inside, in different shapes.

items.p: In the Floppy Sock Arm activity, the sock with one long ruler inside could point but could not bend. What did it need to bend?
items.a: It needed two bones with a joint between them, like the two pencils.
items.why: A strong answer says that stiff bones hold you up, but bending needs a joint where two bones meet.

items.p: Three cousins are arguing about which joint is the best.

views.says: The shoulder is best. It moves in a whole circle, so I can throw and swim.
The knee is best. It only bends one way, so it stays steady when I stand and jump.
There is no best joint. Each one suits its job.

items.ask: Talk it over. Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another cousin has right. A grown-up writes down your answer.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. Kavya is right that the shoulder moves the most. Meena is right that a hinge is steady: a shoulder can slip out of its cup more easily than a knee or an elbow. Ammu is right that each joint fits what it does.
items.why: A ball and socket joint moves more ways, but it is less steady. A hinge moves fewer ways, but it is steadier. Both kinds are useful in different places.

items.p: Put these bones in order, from the longest to the shortest.
items: a tiny bone in the ear
a: a tiny bone in the ear
items.why: The thigh bone is the longest bone in the body. The upper arm bone is shorter. Finger bones are small, and the tiniest bone, in the ear, is smaller than a grain of rice.

items.p: True or false: a muscle can push a bone as well as pull it.
items.why: False. A muscle can only get shorter and pull. To move a joint back, a different muscle on the other side pulls.

items.p: Remember the Muscle Feel activity. Draw your upper arm muscle when your arm is straight, and when you lift the bottle.
items.a: A long thin muscle when the arm is straight, and a short fat bump when the arm is bent.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the muscle getting shorter and fatter as it pulls the forearm up.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, one labelled straight arm and one labelled bent arm.

items.p: The strong cord that joins your calf muscle to your heel bone is a ___.
items.why: A tendon joins a muscle to a bone. You can feel this one at the back of your ankle when you stand on tiptoe.

items.p: A pigeon's leg seems to bend backwards. Which of your joints is that bend like? How can you show it with your own leg?
items.a: It is like my ankle. If I stand on tiptoe, my heel goes up and my ankle bends like the pigeon's leg.
items.why: A strong answer names the ankle and says that birds stand on their toes with the heel up.

items.p: Label the arm: shoulder, elbow, wrist. Then write H next to each hinge joint and B next to each ball and socket joint.
a: wrist: neither, it is in between
items.why: The shoulder is a ball and socket joint and the elbow is a hinge. The wrist moves up and down and side to side, so it is in between.
items.art: A drawing of an arm held out sideways, with three empty label lines at the shoulder, the elbow and the wrist.

items.p: True or false: to bend your elbow, the muscle at the back of your upper arm gets short and hard.
items.why: False. The muscle at the front of your upper arm gets short and hard and pulls the forearm up. The muscle at the back pulls to straighten the arm.

items.p: A tennis player's hitting arm has thicker bones than her other arm. Why?
opts: Bone cells build more bone where the body pushes on it most
She eats more than other people
Bones grow thicker if you do not use them
items.why: Bone is alive. Bone cells build more bone where it is pushed and pressed, so a hard-working arm gets stronger bones.

items.p: Say your answer out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. Suppose your knee was a ball and socket joint, like your hip. What new things could you do? What could go wrong?
items.a: I could swing my lower leg round in a circle. But my knee might wobble or slip when I stand or jump.
items.why: A strong answer gives one thing gained, more ways to move, and one thing lost, a steady knee to stand on.

items.p: Revathi, her cousin Anitha and her aunt are talking about whether bones are alive.

views.says: Bones are alive. A broken arm mends by itself in a few weeks.
A skeleton in a museum is bone, and it is not alive. So bone is not alive.
The hard part of bone is made of minerals, a bit like chalk. Living bone cells live inside it and keep building it.

items.ask: Talk it over. Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right. A grown-up writes down your answer.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view with a reason. Revathi is right that a living bone mends. Anitha is right that a museum skeleton is no longer alive, because the bone cells have died. The aunt explains both: the hard part is mineral, and the cells inside it are alive.
items.why: Bone in a living body is alive, because it has living cells and blood. When an animal dies, the cells die, and the hard mineral part is left.

items.p: Astronauts who live in space for months come back with weaker bones. Why?
opts: In space, nothing presses on their bones, so bone cells build less bone
There is no food in space
Their bones melt in the cold
items.why: Bone cells build bone where it is pushed and pressed. In space, the body has no weight pressing down, so some bone is lost. Astronauts exercise every day to slow this.

items.p: Design a robot arm that must stir a pot of sambar round and round. Draw it, and mark which joints are hinges and which are ball and socket joints.
items.a: An arm with at least one ball and socket joint or a turning joint, so the spoon can go round.
items.why: A strong design uses a ball and socket joint, or a joint that turns, because stirring needs a circle. Hinges alone only go back and forth.
items.art: An empty box with a pot drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Say your answer out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. Many people say that cracking your knuckles is bad for your joints. How could you test this?
items.a: One person cracks the knuckles of only one hand for many years. Then a doctor checks both hands and compares them.
items.why: A strong answer compares two groups or two hands that are the same except for the cracking. A doctor named Donald Unger did this with his own hands for about 60 years and found no difference.

items.p: True or false: a newborn baby has more separate bones than a grown-up.
items.why: True. A newborn baby has about 300 bones and bits of bone. Many of them join together as the child grows, until a grown-up has about 206.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to a true fact about their skeleton.
pairs: the backward bend in the leg is the ankle
has a hard skeleton on the outside
has a backbone and ribs inside
items.why: Giraffes and humans are both mammals with 7 neck bones. Birds stand on their toes. Ants have no bones, and their hard skeleton is outside. Fish have a backbone, like us.
items.art: A giraffe, a crow, an ant and a fish on the left, and four short facts on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Label the finger drawing: bone, joint, tendon.
a: bone: the stiff parts between the bends
joint: the places where the finger bends
tendon: the cord along the finger that pulls it
items.why: The bones are stiff, the joints are where it bends, and the tendons are pulled by muscles in the forearm to curl the finger.
items.art: A side drawing of a finger with its three bones, the joints between them, and a cord running along the underside, with three empty label lines.

items.p: In the Torch on the Wall experiment, the torch light drew a line or a circle. Sort these joints by which one they can draw.
items.why: The knee, elbow and middle finger joint are hinges, so they move one way and back. The hip and shoulder are ball and socket joints, so they can go round.

items.p: Say your answer out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. In the Bone Hunt, you felt ribs over your chest but no bone at the front of your tummy. Why might a body be built that way?
items.a: The ribs keep my heart and lungs safe. My tummy needs to bend when I bend over, and to stretch when I eat a big meal.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason for both: soft parts that need guarding get bone, and parts that must bend and stretch do not.

quiz.p: What do we call the hard, living parts inside your body?
quiz.why: Bones are the hard parts inside you. Muscles are soft and can pull. Skin covers the outside.

quiz.p: About how many bones does a grown-up have?
quiz.why: A grown-up has about 206 bones. A newborn baby has more pieces, about 300, and many of them join as the child grows.

opts: A place where two bones meet
quiz.why: A joint is where two bones meet. Your body bends at its joints.

quiz.p: Your elbow bends and straightens like a door. What kind of joint is it?
quiz.why: A hinge joint moves one way and back, like a door. The elbow and knee are hinge joints.

quiz.p: Which of these joints can move round in a circle?
quiz.why: The hip is a ball and socket joint, like the shoulder. The knee and elbow are hinges.

opts: Keep your heart and lungs safe
quiz.why: The ribs make a cage of bone round the heart and lungs.

quiz.p: What would a body be like with no bones at all?
quiz.why: Bones hold the body up. Without them, a body would flop, like the empty sock in the Floppy Sock Arm activity.

quiz.p: How does a muscle move a bone?
quiz.why: Muscles can only pull. They get shorter and harder as they pull a bone.

quiz.p: A nurse puts a plaster cast on a broken arm. Why?
opts: To keep the pieces still while the bone cells mend it
Because the cast makes new bone
quiz.why: Bone is alive. Bone cells build new bone across the crack. The cast only holds the pieces still so they join straight.

quiz.p: Why can a broken bone mend, when a cracked stone cannot?
opts: Bone is alive and has living cells
quiz.why: Living bone cells build new bone. A stone has no living cells, so a crack in a stone stays.

applications: Doctors take X-rays to see if a bone is broken, and to check that it has mended straight.
Bone doctors, called orthopaedic doctors, put plaster casts on broken bones to keep them still while they heal.
Doctors can replace a worn-out hip or knee with a new joint made of metal and plastic.
Engineers copy the hinge and ball and socket joints of the body in door hinges, robot arms and the joints of lamps and camera stands.
Physiotherapists help people move stiff joints and make weak muscles strong again after an injury.
Scientists who study fossils use the shapes of bones to work out how animals that lived long ago moved.

open_questions.q: How exactly do bone cells feel the pushes of running and jumping, and pass the message on?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that bone cells sense pressure and send signals to build more bone. Exactly how they sense it is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why does a broken bone heal with new bone, while a deep cut in skin often leaves a scar?
open_questions.why_open: Bone can rebuild itself very well. Scientists are still learning why bone mends so well and skin does not, and hope to use this to help other parts heal.

open_questions.q: Why do almost all mammals, from mice to giraffes, have 7 neck bones?
open_questions.why_open: Only a few mammals, such as sloths and manatees, have a different number. Scientists have ideas about why, but nobody is sure.

maths.problem: In the Bend and Dot activity, each finger had 3 bones and the thumb had 2. How many bones are in the fingers and thumb of one hand?
maths.explain: Four fingers with 3 bones each: 3, 6, 9, 12. Add the thumb's 2 bones: 12 and 2 make 14.
maths.context: This is about the Bend and Dot activity, where you counted the bones in your fingers.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups of 3 is quicker than counting every bone one by one.

maths.problem: If one hand has 14 bones in its fingers and thumb, how many are in the fingers and thumbs of both hands?
maths.context: This is about the bones you counted in your fingers in the Bend and Dot activity.
maths.why_maths: Your two hands are the same, so doubling one hand gives both, without counting again.

maths.problem: In the Bone Hunt, a child made 9 red dots for hard bone and 5 blue dots for soft. Did the child find more hard places or more soft places, and how many more?
maths.explain: Count on from 5 to 9: 6, 7, 8, 9. That is 4 more red dots than blue dots.
maths.context: This is about the Bone Hunt, where you pressed 14 places and coloured red or blue dots.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts shows that, in the places on the list, bone near the skin was more common than soft parts.

maths.problem: A giraffe has 7 neck bones. You have 7 neck bones. A giraffe's neck is much longer than yours. What must be different about the giraffe's neck bones?
maths.answer: Each of the giraffe's neck bones is much longer.
maths.explain: The number is the same: 7 and 7. So the extra length must come from the size of each bone, not from more bones.
maths.context: This is about the card on skeletons in other animals.
maths.why_maths: When two numbers are the same but the lengths differ, the difference must be in the size of each part.

maths.problem: A child is 120 centimetres tall. The thigh bone is about one quarter of a person's height. About how long is the child's thigh bone?
maths.explain: One quarter is half of a half. Half of 120 is 60. Half of 60 is 30. So the thigh bone is about 30 centimetres, as long as a school ruler.
maths.context: This is about the Life-Size Bone Map, where you measured your bones with string.
maths.why_maths: A quarter of your height tells you roughly how long your thigh bone is, without needing to see inside.
