science: Adult skeleton about 206 bones; newborn about 270 to 300 ossification centres and bones that fuse with growth; hand 27 bones (14 phalanges), foot 26; femur longest, stapes smallest (about 3 mm); femur about one quarter of stature. Standard anatomy texts (Gray's Anatomy).

Joint types: shoulder and hip ball and socket (spheroidal) joints; elbow (humero-ulnar) and knee mainly hinge joints; interphalangeal joints hinges; wrist (radiocarpal), metacarpophalangeal joints and ankle complex allow movement in two planes. Forearm rotation at the radio-ulnar joints.
Patella is cartilage at birth and ossifies from about age 3 to 6. Anterior fontanelle closes at about 18 to 24 months. Mandible forms in two halves that fuse at the symphysis in the first year.

Bone remodelling and mechanosensing by osteocytes; bone mass loss in microgravity (about 1 to 1.5 percent a month at the hip, NASA); greater bone in the playing arm of tennis players (H. H. Jones and colleagues, Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery 59A, 1977).

Galen's statement that the lower jaw is two bones, corrected by Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica (1543). W. C. Röntgen, 'Über eine neue Art von Strahlen' (December 1895); the X-ray of Anna Bertha Röntgen's hand, 22 December 1895.

Knuckle cracking: D. L. Unger, 'Does knuckle cracking lead to arthritis of the fingers?', Arthritis and Rheumatism 41 (1998) 949-950. G. N. Kawchuk and colleagues, 'Real-time visualization of joint cavitation', PLOS ONE 10 (2015) e0119470. A. Unsworth, D. Dowson and V. Wright, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 30 (1971) 348-358 (bubble collapse). V. Chandran Suja and A. I. Barakat, Scientific Reports 8 (2018) 4600 (partial collapse model).

Sushruta Samhita, Sharira Sthana chapter 5: 300 bones, and eight kinds of joints, including kora (hinge-like: fingers, wrists, ankles, knees, elbows) and ulukhala (mortar-like: shoulders, hips, teeth). Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana chapter 7: 360 bones, counting teeth and nails.
Seven cervical vertebrae in nearly all mammals, including giraffes; exceptions include sloths and manatees. The backward-bending joint in a bird's leg is the ankle (intertarsal joint).

roots.context: We have felt our bones, found our joints and tested which joints can draw a circle. Now we ask what the Torch on the Wall experiment tells us about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Torch on the Wall experiment, when you moved only your elbow, the torch light could only go up and down. When you moved only your shoulder, the light drew a whole circle. The elbow fits together like a door hinge, and the shoulder like a ball in a cup. So the ways your body can move are set by the shapes where its bones meet.
deep_truth.habit: We think of moving as something we simply decide to do, or something our muscles do. But muscles can only pull a bone the ways its joint allows. The shape where the bones meet decides which paths are possible.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Torch on the Wall experiment, the shoulder and hip could draw circles, while the elbow, knee and middle finger joints could only go back and forth. In an X-ray or a skeleton, the top of the arm bone is a round ball in a cup, and the elbow is a hinge.

three.who_am_i: Inside you is a frame of living bones, about 206 in a grown-up. They are joined at many joints and moved by muscles that pull.
three.what_is_life: Your bones are alive. Bone cells feel the pushes of your running and jumping, and build bone thicker where it is pushed most.
three.what_is_this_world: A crow, a cat, a fish and you all have a backbone, a skull and ribs. Many animals share one plan of bones, in different shapes.

roots.thread: Bone cells feel the pressing of your weight and the jolts of your jumping. They answer by building bone where it is needed and taking it away where it is not. So the shape of your bones is a record of how you have lived and moved. Some scientists call this an automatic response to pressure.

teachings.teaching: Sushruta, a surgeon in ancient India, named the joints of the body by their shapes. He called the joints of the fingers, knees and elbows kora, like a hinge. He called the joints of the shoulders and hips ulukhala, like a mortar with its pestle.
teachings.link: The Torch on the Wall experiment found the same thing: the hinge joints swing one way, and the shoulder and hip turn in a cup like a pestle in a mortar.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching, an old Chinese book, says that a living person is soft and bending, and a dead body is stiff and hard. A living plant is soft and bends, and a dead one is dry and breaks.
teachings.link: This unit says something similar: life goes with moving and changing. A living body bends at its joints, and living bone is always being rebuilt. A museum skeleton is hard and still, because its living cells have died.

science.text: Bone is living. Bone cells build and remove bone all through life, and build more bone where it is pressed and pushed.
Exactly how bone cells sense pressure and pass the message to other cells is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Many biologists say bone cells do not listen or answer in any way like a person does. They say the cells follow chemical rules when they are squeezed, the way a switch turns on when it is pressed.

practice.title: Joint by Joint
practice.say: Sit or stand comfortably. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out. Now wiggle only your toes. Now draw a slow circle with one ankle. Now bend and straighten one knee. Now draw a big slow circle with your arm from the shoulder. Bend your elbow and straighten it. Last, curl your fingers and open them. Breathe out. Which joints went round? Which only bent?
practice.kid: Breathe in slowly. Breathe out. Wiggle your toes. Draw a circle with your ankle. Bend your knee. Swing your arm in a big circle. Bend your elbow. Curl your fingers. Which ones went round?

ask: If your joints were all ball and socket joints, would that be better or worse? Why?

how_we_found_out.story: About 1,850 years ago, a famous Greek doctor called Galen worked in Rome. People there were not allowed to cut open human bodies to study them. So Galen studied the bodies of monkeys, pigs, dogs and other animals instead. He wrote that the human lower jaw is two bones, joined at the chin. In dogs and many other animals, it is. For about 1,300 years, doctors in Europe learnt from Galen's books, and few checked. In 1543, a young doctor named Andreas Vesalius, who taught in Padua in Italy, published a big book of drawings made from real human skeletons. He showed that a grown-up's lower jaw is one bone. A baby's jaw starts as two halves, but they join in the first year. Vesalius showed that the only way to know is to look at the real thing. Then, in 1895 in Germany, Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays. One of his first X-ray pictures was of his wife Anna Bertha's hand. For the first time, people could see the bones inside a living person.
how_we_found_out.who: Galen, Andreas Vesalius, and Wilhelm Röntgen with Anna Bertha Röntgen
how_we_found_out.when: About 170 CE (Galen), 1543 (Vesalius) and 1895 (the first X-ray pictures)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the human lower jaw is two bones, because Galen studied the jaws of other animals. Vesalius looked at real human skeletons and showed that an adult's jaw is one bone.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in a long 1890s dress resting her hand on a photographic plate, and beside it the grey X-ray picture of her hand bones with a ring on one finger.
